newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes $43 million for food safety.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes $43 million for food safety.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday proposed spending $43 million to make the nation's food supply safer by tracking food-borne illnesses more aggressively and inspecting seafood more rigorously.

Announcing the idea in his weekly radio address, Clinton recalled the contaminated apple juice that killed one child in the Pacific Northwest last year and a 1993 outbreak of the E. coli bacteria in hamburgers that killed four children.

"No parent should have to think twice about the juice they pour their children at breakfast, or a hamburger ordered during dinner out," Clinton said in a text of the address released by the White House. "Hard-working American parents deserve the peace of mind that comes from knowing that the meal they set before their children is safe."
The White House said that Clinton's plan, which is to be included in his new budget proposal on Feb. 6 and which would have to be passed by Congress, included several steps:
-- giving $23 million to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to boost seafood inspections;

-- spending $11.5 million to expand the "early warning" system to track food-borne illnesses by boosting the number of "sentinel sites" around the country that track such outbreaks to eight from five; of this, $10 million would go to the Centers for Disease Control to track the resulting data;
-- giving $8.5 million to the Department of Agriculture for food-safety research, training and education.

The money would help fund state-of-the-art technology to investigate contamination, including genetic "finger-printing" to identify infectious agents, as well as to hire more expert "disease detectives" to track outbreaks to their source.

The food-safety initiative is Clinton's second in the past six months. In July, he announced new regulations that begin to take effect next week to modernize the nation's meat and poultry inspection for the first time in 90 years.
Consumer groups, reacting to outlines of the proposal released on Friday, welcomed the news.

"This is a badly needed shot in the arm for the FDA -- they have suffered under tremendous funding deficiencies for food safety inspections," said Carolyn Smith De Waal of the Center for Science in the Public Interest.

The Agriculture Department is responsible for inspecting meat and poultry, but the job of overseeing the safety of the millions of pounds of seafood Americans eat every year falls to the FDA. Consumer activists have long complained of an inadequate seafood inspection system due to lack of funding.

"Agriculture Department inspectors are in meat and poultry plants every single day, but the FDA is in seafood plants at best once a year, and at worst maybe only once every three years," De Waal added.
